description: A 7th straight quarter of triple-digit growth, a raised full-year guide, and Mr. Market the stock back at a steep discount anyway. I kept the target, kept the BUY, and added to the position.
body_html:
Last week we saw a divergence between two positions. DELL was the top performer in the portfolio, while CRDO was the worst performer.

On Sunday, I published my view on DELL, lowered the target price from $639 to $601, read as to why here.

Today I trimmed DELL from 11% to 8.5% and put the proceeds into CRDO, taking it from 4% to 6%.

Since adding this position and before the rebalancing, it was up 127%. Three weeks ago it was up 276%.

Revenue more than doubled y/y, above the top of its own guidance range, a 48% operating margin, full-year growth guide raised. The stock fell the next day and dropped further the day after. From its peak to the bottom, there was a significant drawdown, on a quarter with nothing that would justify it in my opinion.

Table of Contents

  • How the stock ranks

  • Q1 FY2027: a record quarter that got sold

  • Guidance: what changed since June

  • Thesis scorecard after Q1 FY2027

  • Valuation: the $315 target, rebuilt

  • The Monte Carlo: 10,000 runs

  • Risk register after Q1 FY2027

  • Verdict

TLDR

  • CRDO’s Q1 FY2027 revenue grew +115% y/y and +10% sequentially, above the top of the guided range; non-GAAP EPS was in line. It was the seventh consecutive quarter of triple-digit growth.

  • Guidance went up: FY2027 revenue growth from more than 80% to more than 85%, Q2 guided +10% to +12% sequentially against the mid-single digits promised in June. Opex guidance rose too, from +50% to +55%.

  • The stock fell 27% in two sessions and 40% from its August high. Peers and the semiconductor index were flat to up over the same days. This was a CRDO-specific derating, and the reason is the shape of the year: the second half has to average $730M a quarter for the guide to hold.

  • Thesis scorecard: three pillars confirmed, two evolving. Optics and customer breadth are the two still being proven, and the first one carries the year.

  • The DCF is unchanged at $315. Against a $74 bear case the risk/reward is 1 to 1.5. CRDO stays a BUY, and I added to the position today, taking it from 4% to 6%.

How the stock ranks

RankedStocks.com scores CRDO at RS 67, down 7 points in a week to its lowest reading since June.

The drop came from Sentiment; Valuation improved 5 points because the price fell, and the operating scores did not move.

Growth 99. Every trailing line is in the top decile and the forward lines score higher still. The one yellow cell is the 3-5 year EPS growth estimate; note that it is estimating a CAGR of +35%, but it is low compared to its peers.

Profitability 82. Margins and returns on capital sit at the top of the group. The three red cells are the ones the bears are pointing at this week: capex to sales, asset turnover and cash from operations, all of which reflect the working-capital build for the second half and the goodwill that arrived with the DustPhotonics acquisition.

Valuation 15. Every multiple except PEG scores in the bottom quartile of the sector, and that is after a 40% fall. The PEG row is the whole debate in one line: expensive on what it earned, cheap on what it is guided to earn.

Against its peer group, CRDO now sits seventh of ten on the composite, with a forward revenue CAGR only Sandisk [] and Astera Labs [] match, a forward EBIT margin nobody in the table matches, and a Valuation score above only ALAB and Ciena [].

You can run the same work on any ticker yourself, for free, at RankedStocks.com.

Q1 FY2027: a record quarter that got sold

Revenue grew +115% y/y and +10% sequentially, above the top of the guided range and 1.2% above consensus.

Non-GAAP EPS of $1.20 came in 2.6% above consensus, which I treat as in line.

Non-GAAP gross margin was 68%, the midpoint of the range, and operating margin was 48.2%. Non-GAAP net income grew +140% y/y. Cash flow from operations was $90M and FCF $83M, down from $178M in the April quarter.

AECs still did the work. Unit shipments of AECs contributed more than 90% of the $256M y/y revenue increase. Optical DSPs and retimers each posted record revenue, and the first silicon photonics revenue from DustPhotonics landed in the quarter, but in dollars this was still an AEC quarter. AEC growth is slowing from the doubling and tripling of the last two years, and optics grows faster from a smaller base. So the product carrying the numbers today is decelerating while the product carrying the guide has three months of shipments behind it.

The GAAP line is where the sell-off came from. Non-GAAP gross margin held at 68%; GAAP gross margin fell from 68.2% to 64.5%, because the DustPhotonics intangibles now amortize through cost of revenue at $58M a year at the current run rate. GAAP operating expenses rose from $89.6M a year ago to $188.4M, with $82M of that share-based compensation, so GAAP operating income of $121M was down 22.5% from the April quarter while revenue rose 10%. Non-GAAP opex also came in above the top of the guided range for the third quarter in a row, up 16% sequentially. None of this is new information (the acquisition closed in May, and the SBC line has grown with the headcount for years), but the first quarter where the GAAP income statement went backwards was always going to be read badly by anyone screening on it, and the sell side did exactly that: the print was described as “solid” with a revenue beat and guide that “seems a bit skinnier” than prior quarters. Skinnier is the right word. The last three revenue beats against the top of the range were 18%, 0.5% and 0.8%.

Cash went to the ramp. Working capital absorbed $151M in the quarter: receivables up $55M and inventory up $62M to $313M, ahead of the second-half shipments. On top of that, CRDO has $88M of refundable capacity deposits with assembly subcontractors and signed another $102M after quarter end, in exchange for reserved capacity on two- to six-year agreements. Cash and short-term investments fell $679M to $764M, almost all of it the $735M net cash paid for DustPhotonics. Total consideration for the deal was $1.25B, of which $896M is goodwill and $310M is an earn-out. Debt is $21M.

Concentration is easing, slowly. The top four end customers were 33%, 28%, 13% and 10% of revenue, 84% combined against 87% in the April quarter, and the fourth name changed from the prior quarter. A year ago the top three alone were 88%. The 10-Q reports by billing customer rather than end customer, and on that basis the concentration looks heavier. The receivable balance is the sharper reading, and it moved the wrong way in the quarter.

Revenue shipped to mainland China went from $52M a year ago to $1M.

Was it the sector? No. Over the four sessions from the print to Friday’s close, the semiconductor index [SMH], ALAB and Marvell [MRVL] rose while CRDO fell.

Guidance: what changed since June

Every operating line in that table moved up or stayed put. So why the drawdown? The second-half explains it.

FY2026 revenue was $1.34B, so more than 85% growth means at least $2.47B. Q1 plus the Q2 midpoint is $1.01B, which leaves at least $1.46B for the second half, an average of $730M a quarter against a Q2 guide of $530M. That is a 38% step up between the second and the third quarter, and it has to come mostly from ZeroFlap optical modules, silicon photonics and 1.6T DSPs, products that are a small slice of the revenue you can see today.

On credibility, the record is clean in one direction and consistently sloppy in the other. Revenue has come in above the top of the guided range for four consecutive quarters. Non-GAAP opex has come in above the top of its range for three consecutive quarters. So management under-promises on revenue and under-budgets R&D. I take the >85% as a floor and I add a few points to the opex line in the model.

Thesis scorecard after Q1 FY2027

My CRDO thesis was built on four legs: active electrical cables becoming the default short-reach connection inside AI clusters, optics turning into a second growth engine on the same system-level playbook, a customer base widening beyond the first hyperscaler, and a cost structure that turns 68% gross margins into 50% net margins. The fifth leg, as always, was that the price did not reflect the first four.

Here is where each leg stands.

Pillar #1. AECs are the short-reach default, and CRDO owns the category: Confirmed, normalizing

Original thesis: copper with a chip in it beats laser optics on reliability and power inside the rack and up to seven meters, and CRDO’s system-level qualification makes it the supplier of choice as clusters scale.

Evolution: in June the count was five of six hyperscalers deployed at volume, with only xAI described as fully penetrated.

What happened since the last update: AECs contributed more than 90% of the y/y revenue increase in Q1. Five hyperscalers remain, neocloud engagement expanded, and 1.6T AECs are expected to contribute in the second half of FY2027 and “in a much bigger way” in FY2028. Marvell’s Golden Cable program, which hands Foxconn and Luxshare reference designs to bring their own AECs to market in months, is live, and its first 1.6T design took two months.

Assessment: the pillar holds, and the growth rate is coming down from tripling to something that still doubled y/y. The competition is now real at the component level, which is why the ASP uplift at 200G per lane and the PILOT telemetry layer matter more than they did in October 2024.

Pillar #2. Optics as the second engine: Evolving

Original thesis: the AEC playbook (own the SerDes, own the DSP, harden the whole link, sell reliability) transfers to optical modules, where link flaps cost hyperscalers GPU utilization.

Evolution: June set the number: more than $600M of optical revenue in FY2027 across optical DSPs, silicon photonics and ZeroFlap modules, each above $100M.

What happened since the last update: the $600M was reiterated. Optical DSPs hit record revenue, first PIC revenue was recognized, production shipments of ZeroFlap modules are underway with hyperscalers and neoclouds, and the DustPhotonics team landed two design wins with “major players” for FY2028 ramps. CRDO also joined the OCP consortium for near-package optics, with scale-up design wins expected to ramp in FY2028. The first 1.6T DSP revenue remains a second-half event.

Assessment: every milestone that could be hit in three months was hit, and the one that matters, $600M of shipments, is still ahead. This stays Evolving until the October quarter prints, and it is the pillar the whole year rests on.

Pillar #3. A widening customer base: Evolving

Original thesis: from one anchor hyperscaler to several, plus the neocloud tier, bringing the top-customer share down over time.

Evolution: a year ago the top three were 35%, 33% and 20%. In June they were 34%, 27% and 16%, with a fourth crossing 10% for the first time.

What happened since the last update: 33%, 28%, 13% and 10%, with a different fourth name. Two customers are 61% of revenue, four are 84%, and by billing customer the largest is 43%. China revenue is gone. Management repeats that three to four customers will stay above 10% and that neoclouds could reach 20% of revenue over time.

Assessment: the trend is the right one (the top three went from 88% to 74% in a year) but the level is still very concentrated. The neocloud tier is the swing factor, and it has not shown up as a 10% customer yet. Evolving.

Pillar #4. The cost structure converts growth into cash: Confirmed, with an asterisk

Original thesis: a fabless model with 68% gross margins and R&D growing far slower than revenue produces net margins near 50% and a growing net cash pile.

Evolution: FY2026 delivered a 51.9% non-GAAP net margin in Q4 and a record $178M of quarterly FCF.

What happened since the last update: 49.3% non-GAAP net margin in Q1, opex above plan again, FCF down to $83M on a $151M working-capital build, and $190M of capacity deposits either paid or committed. GAAP margins fell on acquisition accounting and $88M of stock compensation.

Assessment: the earnings engine is intact and the cash conversion took a quarter off to fund the second half. The asterisk is SBC: at 18% of revenue it is a real cost that the non-GAAP margin ignores.

Pillar #5. The price does not reflect the first four: Confirmed

Original thesis: at $75 the market was pricing a niche cable vendor.

Evolution: by June the stock was $226 and by August 17 it was $283; the target did not move.

What happened since the last update: the stock fell to $171. At the August high the setup was $283 against $315, with almost no room for error. Today it is $171 against $315 and a $74 bear, a risk/reward of 1 to 1.5. The reverse DCF says $171 prices 21% annual revenue growth over the decade against the 35% the Street models.

Assessment: the mispricing is back. Three weeks ago I would have had CRDO on the trim list; the market did the trimming for me.

Valuation: the $315 target, rebuilt

The target is unchanged at $315, but the model underneath it is new, so this section is longer than usual for an update. I rebuilt the DCF on RankedStocks.com from the FY2026 base year with ten explicit years, and you can open every input here.

Five assumptions carry the number.

First, revenue. FY2027 grows 88%, on top of the >85% guide and inside the Street’s $2.25B-$2.55B range. FY2028 grows 60% to $4.0B, which is a full year of the three optical lines, the 1.6T AEC transition and first revenue from near-package optics, active LED cables and OmniConnect memory gearboxes, and it is still inside the Street’s range.

From FY2029 my model parts company with consensus: +45%, +32% and +24% put FY2031 revenue at $9.5B against a Street average of $6.0B and a high of $6.8B. This is where the $315 comes from. The defence is that the Street’s FY2030 estimate grows 7%, which is a placeholder from a thin panel rather than a forecast, that management describes FY2027 as “a stepping stone” with outsized growth through 2030, and that the pluggable transceiver market alone is forecast to go from 60M units in 2026 to 175M in 2030 (per the industry trackers management cites) before counting scale-up optics or the $2,000-$3,000 of OmniConnect content per inference GPU that starts shipping in FY2028. Ten-year revenue CAGR in the base is 28%; revenue in FY2036 is $15.7B.

Second, margins, and here I have to make a choice. The inputs are on the same basis management guides: 68% gross margin through FY2030 fading to 65% by FY2036, operating expenses at 20% of revenue in FY2027 (a little above the +55% opex guide, for the reasons in the credibility paragraph) falling to 17.5%. That gives a 48% operating margin in FY2027, rising to 50% and fading to 47.5%.

Third, tax at 8% rising to 15%, the global minimum, against the 0% to 3% the Cayman structure has actually paid.

Fourth, reinvestment: capex and D&A set equal at 3.2% of revenue fading to 2.2%, which is above reported capex because the capacity deposits behave like capex, and inventory days coming down from 185 to 130 as the pre-build for the ramp unwinds.

Fifth, the discount rate. The company has $21M of debt, so the WACC is the cost of equity: a 4.8% risk-free rate plus a 1.2 beta times a 4.2% equity risk premium, 9.7%. The regression beta of 3.2 describes the stock, not the business; Damodaran’s semiconductor beta is 1.5 and at that rate the same case is worth $260. Terminal growth is 3%, the terminal value is 62% of enterprise value and the implied exit multiple is 11.7x EBIT.

I always like to do the exercise of getting to the market price by playing with the DCF assumptions. Keep every margin and the 9.7% rate, and $171 is the fair value if FY2027 grows 60% instead of the guided 85%+, FY2028 grows 41%, FY2029 grows 31%, and FY2031 revenue lands at $5.6B, below the Street average. In other words, Mr. Market is pricing a miss on the full year, and then a business that never catches up to what the sell side already has in its models. That is a strong claim to make about a company that has beaten the top of its own range four quarters in a row.

The second-half optical inflection half-delivers and FY2027 revenue lands at $2.3B (+72%, a clear miss against the guide), Marvell’s cable partners take AEC share during the 1.6T transition so FY2028 grows only 25%, one of the two big customers digests in FY2029 (+10%), and CRDO settles into a 5% to 8% grower with gross margin eroding to 61% and operating margin to 35%. Same discount rate. That is $74 per share, 57% below today. Against $144 of upside to $315 it is a risk/reward of 1 to 1.5.

The Monte Carlo: 10,000 runs

Nine runs in ten land above today’s price and none of them goes to zero. The distribution is right-skewed, which is what a business with a long option tail and no debt should produce, and it is why the mean sits well above the median. The left edge is the part that matters. The fifth percentile sits a hair below where the stock trades today, so Mr. Market has CRDO priced at the bottom of my own assumption set.

Revenue growth does most of the work and the discount rate does most of the rest. Margins, terminal growth and capex are rounding errors in the spread. So the bet here is on whether the optical ramp and the second-half step-up are real, rather than on a margin call or a rate call.

The dispersion is deliberately wide. A 5-point standard deviation on a 30.2% ten-year growth average puts a fifth of the runs below 25% and a fifth above 35%, which brackets both the Street’s number and mine. A full point on the WACC puts the Damodaran sector beta case and a cheaper-capital case inside the same sample.

Risk register after Q1 FY2027

First, the second half. This is the risk, and everything else is a footnote to it. The guide needs $1.46B of revenue in two quarters from products with one quarter of shipments behind them, built at contract manufacturers on 3nm silicon and lasers that the whole industry is fighting over. The capacity deposits and the inventory build say management is leaning in on supply; the demand side is a handful of hyperscaler qualification calendars that CRDO does not control. A slip of one quarter costs the year.

Second, concentration. Two customers at 61% of revenue and one at 43% by billing entity. The counterparties are the best-funded companies on earth, so the risk is order timing rather than credit, but a single deployment pause at the largest customer is a double-digit revenue hole in a quarter.

Third, AECs are no longer a category of one. MRVL’s cable-partner program and Broadcom [] both sell into the same racks, and the CEO conceded on the call that the component level is “quite competitive”. The moat is the qualification rigor and the PILOT telemetry, and I expect CRDO to keep the reliability-sensitive customers and to lose price on the rest. That is already in the margin fade; a faster fade is not.

Fourth, the GAAP arithmetic. SBC at 18% of revenue, $896M of goodwill and a $310M earn-out from an acquisition that is three months old, and a GAAP operating income line that fell 22% sequentially. None of it changes the cash economics this year, but if the optical ramp slips, the goodwill becomes a headline. Form 4s also show the COO and the CTO’s family trust selling through the summer.

Fifth, the tape. A beta above 3, a Fed that is openly discussing a hike, and a new round of semiconductor tariffs under consideration in Washington. Management’s guide is explicitly “based on the current tariff regime, which remains fluid”.

One risk comes off the list. In June I flagged the $750M cash outlay for DustPhotonics as a balance-sheet question. The deal closed, first revenue is booked, two FY2028 design wins are in hand and there is still $764M of cash and no debt. The acquisition is now an execution question.

Verdict

CRDO stays a BUY with the target unchanged at $315. I added to the position today at $171.79, funded by trimming DELL from 11% to 8.5% after I moved it to HOLD on Sunday. CRDO goes from a 4% weight to 6%. At $171 the upside to $315 is $144 against $97 of downside to the $74 bear, a risk/reward of 1 to 1.5.

Three weeks ago Mr. Market paid $283 for a promise of $600M of optical revenue. Today he pays $171 for the same promise plus one more quarter of evidence that it is on schedule. One of those two prices was wrong, and I do not think it was the second one.

If you know someone who sold on September 2 and has been staring at the chart since, share this with them.
